ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði
en: **Hjörleifshöfði** — a **221 m móberg headland** — is named for **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, sworn **blood-brother of Ingólfur Arnarson, Iceland's first settler**. The two **sailed here together around 874**, then split: Ingólfur let the gods choose his home, following his high-seat pillars to Reykjavík; Hjörleifur — who **refused to sacrifice to any god** — parked at the first headland. **His burial mound still crowns the summit.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði
en: Come spring, says *Landnámabók*: **one ox** — so his **enslaved Irishmen dragged the plough**. They killed the ox and **blamed a bear**. Iceland **has no bears** — the newcomers just didn't know that yet. When the Norsemen scattered to hunt it, the thralls **ambushed them one by one**, Hjörleifur included, then fled with the women and boats to the islands offshore.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði
en: Ingólfur found the bodies, tracked the killers to those islands, and killed them all. His eulogy: **“A sad end for a good man, slain by slaves — that's what comes of refusing to sacrifice.”** Those islands became the **Vestmannaeyjar** — **“Isles of the West Men,”** the Norse name for **Irish Gaels** — **named after the enslaved men who did the deed.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði
en: The ghost came **three centuries later**. **Katla**, a fearsome housekeeper at the nearby monastery of **Þykkvabæjarklaustur**, owned **magic breeches that never tired**. Shepherd **Barði** borrowed them; she **drowned him in the whey vat**. When sinking whey threatened to expose the body, she fled onto **Mýrdalsjökull** and **leapt into the chasm still called Kötlugjá — “Katla's rift”** — the volcano's vent. Soon after, a **glacial flood burst from the ice**. **The volcano is named after her** — and every eruption, they say, is her temper.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Hjörleifshöfði

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: In **June 1783** the **Lakagígar** fissure tore open — a **27 km rift of more than 140 vents** — and erupted for **eight months** (the **Skaftáreldar**, “Skaftá Fires”), laying down **14.7 km³ of lava across ~600 km².** That makes it **the second-largest lava flood in historical time, behind Eldgjá** and its **~20 km³** — larger still, but **8,700 years before anyone was here to see it**, is **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**. You're driving across the runner-up.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: And yet the lava barely killed anyone — the **gas** did. The fissure breathed out **~122 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide** plus a fluorine fog that poisoned the grass, and the famine that followed has a name of its own: the **Móðuharðindin, “Mist Hardships.”** The haze even crossed **Europe**, wrecking harvests as far as France.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: The green fuzz is **grámosi**, woolly fringe moss — **decades to grow, one boot-print to wreck.** Admire it through the window.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: The **Skaftáreldar** began on **8 June 1783** and did not stop until **7 February 1784** — eight months to the day, near enough.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: It did not spread politely across country, it went down the rivers: on **11 June** the **Skaftá** simply stopped, and on **3 August** the **Hverfisfljót** went the same way. Two rivers deleted, by something arriving down their own beds.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: Landgræðslan measures that moss mat at an average **38 centimetres** thick, which is also why nothing else grows here — **well over two centuries on**, vascular plants are still sparse, because the mat smothers seeds before they germinate.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: The arithmetic of the **Móðuharðindin**: roughly **10,000 dead — about a fifth of all Icelanders** — the population down from just under **50,000** to just under **40,000** by the end of **1786**, with **smallpox** taking another **1,500** and **earthquakes in August 1784** flattening about **400 farms**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: The haze formed a continuous cloud across the whole northern hemisphere, **30 to 90 degrees of latitude**, depositing **over a tonne of sulphuric acid per square kilometre**. Europe called it the dry fog and spent that summer wondering where it came from.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: The national figure hides the local one. **Vatnajökulsþjóðgarður** puts the livestock loss at **around three quarters of every animal in the country** — and in the worst-hit districts, the ones we have just driven through, **about 40% of the people died.** (One in five is the headline. Out here it was two in five.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Skógafoss → Kirkjubæjarklaustur / Eldhraun
en: One fissure, one very bad year, a whole continent's weather rearranged. The prettiest thing out here is also the deadliest.

en: Behind the two-sisters legend sits one documented case: in **1343** a nun of this house — the sources cannot agree whether **Katrín or Kristín** — was **burned at the stake** for heresy and for having given herself to the devil in writing.

en: **Kirkjugólf** is not weathered flat, it is decapitated — *jökul- og brimsorfið stuðlaberg*, columns planed off by a glacier and scoured by the sea. Protected **náttúruvætti since 1987**, with a **10-metre** exclusion zone and a **50-metre** buffer, so walk to it and do not stand on it.

en: For centuries this was **the gap in the ring**: unbridgeable rivers that could flood without warning. The **Ring Road (Route 1) wasn't finished until 1974**, when the Skeiðará bridge finally welded the country into one loop.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur
en: Then on **4 November 1996** the **Gjálp/Grímsvötn** eruption melted the ice cap and loosed a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood — peaking near **40,000–50,000 m³ a second, briefly rivalling the Amazon.** It **tore a 24-metre section out of Skeiðarárbrú**, twisting steel girders like wire.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur
en: Those **mangled girders now stand as a roadside monument** — Iceland's polite way of saying “we rebuilt it, but don't get comfortable.”

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur
en: The piece that closed the loop was **Skeiðarárbrú**, started **1972** and finished in **July 1974** at **904 metres** — the **longest bridge in Iceland**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur
en: For scale on **1996**: the **Ölfusá at Selfoss** averages **400 cubic metres a second**, so the flood was running at roughly **125 times** that, carrying icebergs the size of vans. Total damage came in around **1.5 billion krónur** at 2007 prices.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur
en: Rebuilding was quick and quietly humiliating: the span went back up at **880 metres** instead of **904**, and in **2017** it was retired altogether — the national record went backwards to **Borgarfjarðarbrúin at 520 metres**, because the river the big one was built for wandered off. ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skeiðarársandur

en: Tucked into the green oasis of **Skaftafell** is **Svartifoss**, a waterfall framed by black **basalt columns** — the very shape that inspired Reykjavík's Hallgrímskirkja. It's a national park (2008) and **UNESCO World Heritage site (2019).**

en: The measured sequence for **Vatnajökull itself** is brutal: **8,723 km² around 1890**, **8,087 km² in 2000**, **7,745 km² in 2014**. ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / Kirkjubæjarklaustur → Fjallsárlón / Skaftafell & Vatnajökull
